children: European natural gas futures surged as much as 6.8% on Wednesday to €80.99/MWh, the highest since January 2023, as escalating attacks in the Middle East continue to choke liquefied natural gas shipments and drive up costs as the winter heating season approaches; benchmark Dutch TTE front-month futures recently traded 4.5% higher at €79.32/MWh in Amsterdam.

Gains for September have now hit 40%, reflecting growing concerns that any prolonged restriction on LNG production and flows in the region could further reduce the availability of LNG cargoes and force European importers to compete more aggressively with Asian buyers for supplies available from other regions as winter nears.

Qatar, the world's second-largest LNG exporter, was forced in March to curb production after Iranian missile strikes damaged two LNG trains at Ras Laffan, the world’s largest LNG export facility; in August, the country's state-owned petroleum company extended its force majeure on contracted supplies for some buyers into early November.

"Unlike with oil, there are no alternative export routes [for the LNG market], such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea or pipelines leading directly to the Gulf of Oman," Commerzbank commodity analyst Norman Liebke said in a note.

Gas storage across the European Union is only ~67% full, below the seasonal average and 13 percentage points lower than a year ago, and the squeeze could become more acute if colder weather boosts Asian heating demand.

The E.U. tried last week to ease concerns over low stockpiles, saying less inventory is needed after Europe diversified away from natural gas since the 2022 energy shock caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

If the Strait of Hormuz stays shut for the rest of the year, Europe's natural gas storage levels could sink as low as 14% by April 1, according to consultant Wood Mackenzie, which would result in huge bills to refill nearly empty storage tanks in a tight market early next year.

However, a strong El Niño weather system is expected to keep winter temperatures in the region higher than normal, which could depress demand, buying more time for the E.U. to wait for LNG flows to return to normal.

title: Europe natural gas prices top €80/MWh for first time since 2023
